blocks.text: “A woman has recurrent bleeding despite a thin endometrium on ultrasound. Discuss further management.”

Postmenopausal bleeding is vaginal bleeding occurring after menopause, conventionally defined as 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea due to cessation of ovarian function, when there is no other physiological or pathological explanation.
It includes:
Spotting.
Pink or brown discharge.
Bleeding after sexual intercourse.
Frank vaginal bleeding.
A single episode or recurrent episodes.
A woman taking menopausal hormone therapy may have expected bleeding depending on the regimen and timing, but unexpected, persistent or heavy bleeding still requires appropriate assessment.
Do not assume that blood noticed when passing urine or stool is vaginal bleeding. Establish the likely source, while arranging urgent assessment if the source remains uncertain or concerning.
A useful OSCE approach is to divide causes into benign, premalignant and malignant conditions.
A common cause. Reduced oestrogen results in thin, fragile vaginal and sometimes endometrial tissues, causing dryness, irritation, contact bleeding or spotting.
A focal growth of endometrial tissue that may cause intermittent bleeding. Ultrasound or hysteroscopy may identify it.

Abnormal proliferation of endometrial glands, with or without atypia. Atypical hyperplasia/endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN) is particularly important because of its association with concurrent or future endometrial cancer.
Endometrial cancer is a major concern. Other possibilities include cervical, vaginal and vulval cancers, as well as less common uterine malignancies.
Cervical or endometrial polyps.
Cervicitis or vaginal inflammation.
Trauma, including sexual trauma.
Uterine fibroids, although they are a less common explanation for new bleeding after menopause.
Hormone replacement therapy (HRT).
Tamoxifen-associated endometrial changes.
Anticoagulant use, which may worsen bleeding but must not be assumed to be the underlying cause.
Bleeding from the urinary or gastrointestinal tract mistaken for vaginal bleeding.
These are particularly important when evaluating PMB.

blocks.text: OSCE point: A woman without obvious risk factors can still have endometrial cancer.
Use a systematic approach.
Introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity.
Explain that you would like to ask about the bleeding and relevant medical history.
Obtain consent and ensure privacy.
Ask about the patient's immediate concerns, particularly fear of cancer.
Ask:
When did the bleeding start?
When was your last menstrual period?
How many years have you been menopausal?
Was this a single episode or has it happened repeatedly?
Was it spotting, brown discharge or frank red bleeding?
How much blood was there?
Were there clots?
How long did the bleeding last?
Was it spontaneous or after sexual intercourse?
Has the bleeding stopped completely?
Has it been increasing in amount or frequency?
High-yield question: “Have you experienced any further bleeding since that episode?”
Recurrent or persistent bleeding warrants further evaluation even if initial investigations were reassuring.
Ask about:
Pain or burning during urination.
Blood in the urine.
Rectal bleeding.
Vaginal discharge or odour.
Vulval sores, irritation or trauma.
Bleeding after intercourse.
Ask about:
Pelvic or abdominal pain.
Abdominal swelling.
Unintentional weight loss.
Reduced appetite or early satiety.
Fever or symptoms of infection.
Fatigue, dizziness or breathlessness if bleeding has been substantial.
Ask about:
Age at menopause.
Use of HRT: formulation, route, duration and adherence.
Whether she has a uterus or has undergone hysterectomy.
Tamoxifen or other relevant medication.
Vaginal oestrogen or other topical treatments.
Previous endometrial hyperplasia or abnormal biopsy.
A woman who has had a total hysterectomy cannot have uterine endometrial bleeding, so the source must be reassessed.
Previous endometrial, cervical, vaginal or vulval disease.
Previous polyps or fibroids.
Previous pelvic surgery or radiotherapy.
Obesity, diabetes and relevant comorbidities.
Family history of endometrial, colorectal or ovarian cancer.
Anticoagulants, antiplatelet medicines and other medications.
Explore the impact of the bleeding, concerns about malignancy, support at home and preferences around investigations.
Explain the examination and obtain consent. Offer a chaperone and ensure appropriate privacy and exposure.
Assess:
Vital signs.
Pallor, if bleeding has been significant.
Weight and body mass index where relevant.
General condition and signs of systemic disease.
Look for:
Abdominal or pelvic masses.
Tenderness.
Distension or ascites.
Organomegaly when relevant.
Inspect the vulva and perineum for:
Atrophy and fragile skin.
Ulceration or lesions.
Trauma.
Evidence of bleeding from the vulval region.
Inspect:
Vaginal walls for atrophy, inflammation, lesions or active bleeding.
Cervix for polyps, ulceration, friability, discharge or a suspicious mass.
The vaginal fornices.
Any visible source of bleeding.
If bleeding is present, describe its apparent origin but recognise that the source may not always be obvious.
Assess:
Uterine size and contour.
Uterine tenderness.
Cervical motion tenderness.
Adnexal masses or tenderness.
Pelvic fixation or nodularity when malignancy is suspected.

“Speculum examination shows atrophic vaginal mucosa with a small amount of blood. The cervix appears grossly normal, with no obvious cervical lesion. Bimanual examination reveals no palpable uterine or adnexal mass. Although atrophy is a possible cause, further assessment is required to exclude endometrial pathology.”
A normal pelvic examination does not exclude endometrial cancer.
The choice of investigations depends on the patient's risk factors, examination findings, bleeding pattern and local clinical pathway.
TVUS assesses the endometrium, uterus and adnexa.
The endometrial thickness is generally measured as the double-layer endometrial echo in the mid-sagittal plane, excluding intracavitary fluid and following the appropriate measurement technique.
For a woman with an initial episode of PMB, a clearly visualised endometrium measuring 4 mm or less is reassuring in many commonly used pathways.
4 mm or less: cancer is less likely, but persistent or recurrent bleeding still requires further assessment.
More than 4 mm: endometrial sampling is generally indicated in a woman with PMB.
Endometrium not adequately visualised: further assessment is needed.
Focal lesion or irregular endometrium: investigate for a polyp or other pathology, often with hysteroscopy and targeted sampling.
A thin endometrium does not override persistent symptoms or strong clinical concern. Some cancers, including certain non-endometrioid subtypes, may not produce marked endometrial thickening.
Endometrial biopsy, often performed with an outpatient sampling device, is used to obtain tissue for histopathology.
It can diagnose:
Benign endometrium.
Endometrial hyperplasia.
Endometrial carcinoma.
Other endometrial pathology.
A biopsy may be inadequate or fail to sample a focal lesion. A benign or insufficient result does not end the evaluation when bleeding persists or recurs.
Hysteroscopy allows direct visualisation of the uterine cavity and targeted biopsy or removal of a focal lesion.
It is particularly useful when:
A polyp or focal abnormality is suspected.
Endometrial sampling is insufficient.
Bleeding persists despite a benign biopsy.
Imaging and biopsy findings are discordant.

blocks.text: If the assessment supports genitourinary syndrome of menopause and concerning uterine pathology has been appropriately excluded:
Offer vaginal moisturisers or lubricants.
Consider low-dose vaginal oestrogen when appropriate.
Address associated urinary and sexual symptoms.
Arrange reassessment if bleeding recurs.
Vaginal oestrogen should not be used as a substitute for evaluating unexplained PMB.
Hysteroscopic removal may be appropriate, particularly if symptomatic or suspicious.
Send the removed tissue for histopathology.
Management depends on whether atypia is present, the patient's overall risk and her preferences.
Hyperplasia without atypia may be managed with progestogen therapy, often a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, and surveillance.
Atypical hyperplasia/EIN requires specialist assessment because concurrent endometrial carcinoma is possible. Hysterectomy is usually definitive for women who do not require fertility preservation.

Refer to a gynaecological oncology team for staging and treatment planning. Treatment commonly involves hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in operable disease, with additional therapy determined by histology, stage and risk.

blocks.text: Manage according to the site and histology, with specialist referral when malignancy is suspected or confirmed.

subsections.subsection_title: Special scenario: PMB in a woman taking HRT

blocks.text: Bleeding may occur depending on the HRT regimen, especially during expected withdrawal bleeding with sequential therapy. However, unexpected bleeding must be assessed in context.
Ask about:
Whether she uses continuous combined or sequential HRT.
When the regimen was started or changed.
Adherence to the progestogen component.
Whether bleeding occurs at the expected time.
Whether bleeding is heavy, persistent or newly developed after a period of amenorrhoea.
Persistent, heavy or otherwise concerning bleeding requires assessment under the applicable HRT and PMB guidance. Do not assume it is simply due to HRT.
Recurrent or persistent postmenopausal bleeding.
Heavy bleeding or haemodynamic compromise.
A suspicious cervical or vaginal lesion.
A thickened, irregular or inadequately visualised endometrium.
An inadequate biopsy with ongoing symptoms.
Unexplained weight loss, pelvic mass or other features suggesting malignancy.
If the patient is unstable because of heavy bleeding, immediate resuscitation and urgent gynaecological assessment take priority over routine outpatient investigations.
Q1. What is the most important malignancy to exclude in PMB?
Endometrial cancer.
Q2. What endometrial thickness is reassuring on TVUS?

A clearly visualised endometrium measuring 4 mm or less is reassuring for many women with an initial PMB episode. It does not exclude malignancy in every circumstance, and persistent or recurrent bleeding still requires evaluation.
Q3. Does every woman with PMB need an endometrial biopsy?

Not necessarily at the first step. TVUS or sampling may be used initially depending on risk and the clinical pathway. Sampling is indicated when the endometrium is thickened, inadequately visualised or otherwise suspicious, and persistent or recurrent bleeding requires further evaluation.
Q4. What if the endometrium is 3 mm but bleeding continues?
Further assessment is needed, often with endometrial sampling and/or hysteroscopy. Do not dismiss recurrent bleeding because the endometrium is thin.
Q5. What if the endometrial biopsy is insufficient?
Interpret the result alongside symptoms and imaging. If the endometrium is thickened, poorly visualised, or bleeding persists or recurs, further investigation is necessary.
Q6. Why is tamoxifen relevant?

Tamoxifen is associated with endometrial changes and increased endometrial cancer risk. Abnormal bleeding in a woman taking tamoxifen requires evaluation; routine endometrial screening of asymptomatic women is generally not recommended.
Q7. Can anticoagulants explain PMB?
They can worsen bleeding, but they do not exclude an underlying uterine, cervical, vaginal or vulval pathology.
Q8. What is the role of hysteroscopy?
It permits direct inspection of the uterine cavity, targeted biopsy and removal of focal lesions such as polyps.
Q9. What are the common benign causes?
Vaginal or endometrial atrophy and endometrial polyps are common benign causes.
Q10. What is the key counselling message?
Most women with PMB do not have cancer, but investigation is essential because early diagnosis of endometrial cancer can improve outcomes.

“This is a postmenopausal woman presenting with vaginal bleeding after a prolonged period of amenorrhoea. I would establish the bleeding pattern, confirm the likely source, assess relevant risk factors and examine the vulva, vagina, cervix, abdomen and pelvis.

“My differential diagnoses include endometrial atrophy, endometrial polyps, hyperplasia, endometrial cancer and cervical or vaginal pathology. I would arrange transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling or other targeted investigations as indicated, ensuring that persistent or recurrent bleeding receives further assessment.”

content_groups.group_title: Example: ultrasound shows a 7 mm endometrium

blocks.text: “This postmenopausal patient has an endometrial thickness of 7 mm, which exceeds the commonly used 4 mm threshold for an initial PMB assessment. I would arrange endometrial sampling and consider hysteroscopy if a focal lesion is suspected or the sample is inadequate. Histology will determine the next management step.”
A 65-year-old woman presents with a second episode of postmenopausal bleeding. Her transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 3 mm. What is the most appropriate next step?

items: A. Reassure her and discharge because the endometrium is thin
B. Prescribe antibiotics without further assessment
C. Arrange further endometrial assessment, such as sampling and/or hysteroscopy
D. Repeat ultrasound in five years
